new_statements.quote: p.115: 'The system of accentuation of Maḏimaḏi differed considerably from the accentuation of the other Kulin languages, which invariably had a heavy stress accent on the first syllable.' p.155: 'In the standard Kulin languages, both eastern and western, as exemplified by Weṛgaia, Wembawemba and Woiwuru, a word can end in any consonant whatsoever ... Narinari is again unlike Maḏimaḏi in this respect and is in agreement with the other Kulin languages: in all the words recorded the accent falls on the first syllable, as in Weṛgaia and Wembawemba.' p.160 (6.2.2.1 Woiwuru): 'as in gargridj [ˈkarkrɪtj] sugar ... waɳendj [ˈwɔɳendj] wombat'; p.235: 'garawaŋ [ˈgaraˌwaŋ] apple-berry ... mariwan [ˈmarɪˌwan] spearthrower'.
new_statements.citation: Hercus, Luise A. 1986. Victorian languages: a late survey (Pacific Linguistics B-77). Canberra: Department of Linguistics, RSPacS, Australian National University.
new_statements.locator: p.115 (sec. 4.2.3 Accentuation, Kulin-level statement); p.155 (ch.5 (d)-(e), Woiwuru listed among the standard Kulin languages); Woiwuru data: sec. 6.2.2 pp.160-161 and Woiwuru vocabulary pp.234-236 (stress-marked transcriptions)
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened via its text layer (Hercus 1986, Victorian languages: a late survey, PL B-77). All four quoted passages are present at the stated locators, differing only by scanned letter-spacing: (1) p.115, sec. 4.2.3 'Accentuation' (Madimadi chapter), txt lines 6437-6440: 'The system of accentuation of Madimadi differed considerably from the accentuation of the other Kulin languages, which invariably had a heavy stress accent on the first syllable.' (2) p.155, Narinari note, (d) Finals (i), txt line 8450-8451: 'In the standard Kulin languages, both eastern and western, as exemplified by Wergaia, Wembawemba and Woiwuru, a word can end in any consonant whatsoever...' and (e) Word-length and accentu…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary stress on the first syllable of the word (the general Kulin pattern Hercus reports from her own recordings); in her Woiwuru transcriptions every polysyllable carries initial primary stress, with a secondary stress on the third syllable of words of three or more syllables.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not stated in prose for Woiwuru; her Woiwuru transcriptions consistently mark secondary stress on the third syllable (e.g. [ˈgalpaˌninjan], [ˈdjɪrəməˌlaŋ], [ˈŋamaˌdjitj]) and on the second member of reduplications ([ˈbalamˈbalam]).
new_statements.exceptions: None for Woiwuru. Hercus notes for Kulin generally that Madimadi (and Wadiwadi) are the exception with conditioned second-syllable stress; song accentuation differs from speech.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level citation forms elicited from the last rememberers (Wandin family, Healesville, 1960s); Hercus stresses the Woiwuru material is 'so slight that only tentative remarks can be made'. The explicit prose rule is stated for the Kulin languages as a group, not in the Woiwuru section itself; the Woiwuru-specific evidence is her stress-marked phonetic transcriptions.
new_statements.identity_note: Hercus 1986 describes 'Woiwuru' = Woiwurrung proper (Wurundjeri, Yarra/Healesville-Coranderrk), i.e. the Woiwurrung dialect of Glottolog's Woiwurrung-Thagungwurrung (woiw1237); nothing first-hand exists for the Thagungwurrung (Taungurung) or Boonwurrung dialects. Her explicit prose rule is phrased for 'the Kulin languages' (eastern and western, expressly including Woiwuru, p.155); the Woiwuru-specific evidence is her stress-marked transcriptions of c. 80 words from rememberers, all with initial primary stress.

sources.note: First-hand (recorded Wandin family rememberers, Healesville). The Woiwuru section gives a tentative phoneme system and allophone notes referring to 'accented/unaccented' vowels but no sentence on stress position; every Woiwuru word she transcribes (pp.160-161, 234-236) carries primary stress on the first syllable, with secondary stress on the third in longer words (e.g. garawaŋ [ˈgaraˌwaŋ], mariwan [ˈmarɪˌwan], galbaninjan [ˈgalpaˌninjan], djiremelaŋ [ˈdjɪrəməˌlaŋ]). sources.note: Sec. 1.6.1.2 gives Woiwurrung consonants/vowels after Hercus 1986 and Blake 1991 but no stress rule; states initial stress explicitly only for Gippsland (p.27 'every word recorded by Hercus has stress on the initial syllable') and Wemba-Wemba speech vs song; Woiwurrung song accents (Howitt/Torrance acute marks) discussed as musical/linguistic accent, no spoken-word rule.
